rehook_anchors.detail: A bare trunk stands upright among fallen trees. Its branches are gone, yet the wood still points into the sky.
Here is the first discovery: the main destruction fits an explosion in the atmosphere, with the forest struck from above.
In nineteen twenty seven, Leonid Kulik reaches the damaged region. Nineteen years have passed since the fireball crossed the sky.
Now place a compass beside a trunk. Mark the direction from its roots toward its crown, then repeat the observation farther away.
Imagine a rocky body approaching Earth. It carries energy because it is moving, long before a flame becomes visible around it.
Take two equal masses. Double the speed of one, and it carries four times the kinetic energy.
Return to the forest floor. A root plate rises beside a fallen tree, carrying soil that once anchored a heavy trunk.
Look again at the butterfly shape. An incoming body follows a slanting path, carrying momentum while releasing energy into the atmosphere.
Imagine turning a darkened branch toward the daylight. Its surface carries a different question from the direction in which it fell.
Consider a different ordinary object: a tree crown partly hidden behind other trees. Exposure changes which surfaces receive the strongest heating.
It is February the fifteenth, twenty thirteen. A brilliant streak crosses the morning sky near Chelyabinsk, beyond the southern Ural Mountains.
Now place a recovered Chelyabinsk stone beside an image of its recorded trail. One gives material; the other gives a path through time.
A quiet lake offers an appealing possibility. If a surviving fragment struck the ground, perhaps water now covers its cavity.
Imagine a small stone lying among river pebbles. Finding it today supplies a location, but the river has a history.
Fifty million hypothetical encounters. That is the scale explored in one probabilistic study of Tunguska sized impacts published in twenty nineteen.
Strength brings another difference. Two bodies with the same size and speed can fragment differently because their internal structures resist loading differently.
In July twenty twenty four, a Landsat image shows the region covered by forest, marshes, and winding rivers.
Now look upward from the recovering taiga. The atmosphere still receives small bodies from space, most producing little damage below.
Stand once more beside the bare trunk, in a reconstruction of the forest after the event. It has become a pointer.
Lay three images together: an early forest photograph, an atmospheric model, and a camera view of Chelyabinsk.

caveat_beats.text: The forest records the blast; its pattern alone cannot identify the incoming material.
Surveys document damage well, but witnesses and delayed observations leave gaps in detail.
The broad mechanism is established; Tunguska's exact breakup sequence remains a reconstruction.
Terrain and tree condition matter; the map does not determine one exact trajectory.
Burn records constrain the event, but later fires complicate its thermal history.
Chelyabinsk validates key physics, but scaling it up does not uniquely reconstruct Tunguska.
Candidate finds and the Cheko proposal remain disputed; none supplies an agreed identification.
Size and energy remain model dependent; one favored fit is not a recovered body.
A recovered landscape cannot reproduce every original measurement; old records keep their own limits.
The airburst explanation is strong; the body's exact identity remains less securely known.
